case_name: Spence et al. v. Manitoba et al.
text:
Date:  20230630

Docket:  CI 22-01-34789

(Winnipeg Centre)

Indexed as:  Spence et al. v. Manitoba et al.

Cited as:  2023 MBKB 107

COURT OF KING’S BENCH OF MANITOBA

B E T W E E N:

chief
doreen spence, on her own behalf

)

Tim Dickson

AND ON BEHALF OF THE TATASKWEYAK CREE

)

Matthew Boulton

NATION
AND ALL ITS MEMBERS,

)

for the applicants

)

applicants,

)

)

- and -

)

)

THE
MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT, CLIMATE

)

Maureen Killoran, K.C.

AND
PARKS, THE GOVERNMENT OF MANITOBA,

)

Sean Sutherland

AND
THE MANITOBA HYDRO-ELECTRIC BOARD,

)

Brodie Noga

)

for the respondents

respondents.

)

the Minister of Environment,

)

Climate and Parks and

)

the Government of Manitoba

)

)

Joseph M. Langan

)

Gwen L. Muirhead

)

Gavin LeBeau

)

for the respondent

)

Manitoba Hydro-Electric Board

)

)

Judgment delivered

)

June 30, 2023

JOYAL, C.J.K.B.

I.

Introduction

[
1
]

In the context of its underlying application for
judicial review, Tataskweyak Cree Nation (“TCN”) has brought this motion
relating to what TCN identifies as certain deficiencies in the record thus far produced
by the Government of Manitoba (“Manitoba”).  TCN also seeks certain documents
that it says have not been disclosed to it.

[
2
]

The underlying application for judicial review brought
by TCN seeks to quash the decision of the Minister of Conservation and Climate
(the “Minister”) issuing to the Manitoba Hydro‑Electric Board (“Manitoba
Hydro”), a “Final Licence” pursuant to section 43 of the
Waterpower
Regulation
,
M.R. 25/88 R
to
The
Water Power Act
, C.C.S.M.
c. W60, for the Churchill River Diversion (“CRD”) project.  TCN alleges
the decision was made in breach of the Crown’s duty to consult and is accordingly,
unreasonable.

[
3
]

The broader context for this judicial review involving
the allegations by TCN of inadequate consultation and accommodation by Manitoba,
is rooted in concerns about the CRD, a project that diverts much of the
ordinary flow of the Churchill River into another river system (the Nelson
River system) in order to feed hydro-electric dams.

[
4
]

In its motion, TCN seeks three orders.

[
5
]

The first order that TCN seeks relates to what TCN identifies
as unjustified redactions in the Final Licence Record.  This first order would
require Manitoba to produce a copy of the Final Licence Record that is
unredacted except where necessary to protect solicitor-client privilege.  The
redactions that TCN now seeks are more narrow than those that were first identified
in its notice of motion.  Specifically, TCN submits that the following
redactions should not be permitted and that Manitoba should be ordered to
produce a Final Licence Record without them:

(i)

the redactions to the table at pages 22 – 23
that summarizes information relating to Indigenous community participation in
the consultation process;

(ii)

the redactions to the table at pages 23 – 25 of
the Final Licence Record that outlines the consultation budget or funding
agreement that Manitoba offered to each consulted Indigenous community;

(iii)

the redaction of information obtained from
Indigenous communities and groups not party to this proceeding at pages 18, 19,
25 – 26, 95 – 96, and 98 – 108 of the Consultation Report, to the extent such
information would shed light on the adequacy of Manitoba’s consultation with
TCN; and

(iv)

the redaction of the three bullet points at page 55 of the
Consultation Report.

[
6
]

The second order that TCN seeks involves materials that
TCN says were sent to Manitoba during the consultation process and which
expressed concerns about, amongst other things, the CRD and the Augmented Flow Program
(“AFP”).

[
7
]

In respect of this second order, TCN seeks the
inclusion of the following documents that it says are properly part of the
Consultation Record:

(i)

the April 8, 2021 letter from Chief Spence and
Dr. Ian Halket to the Deputy Minister of Conservation and Climate;

(ii)

the April 13, 2021 open letter from TCN and
O-Pipon-Na-Piwin Cree Nation (“OPCN”);

(iii)

the April 15, 2021 op-ed by the Chiefs of TCN
and OPCN in the
Winnipeg Free Press
;

(iv)

the April 21, 2021 correspondence to the
Minister from the Interchurch Council on Hydropower regarding the open letter
and the op-ed;

(v)

the May 10, 2021 correspondence to the Minister
from the Mennonite Church Manitoba regarding the open letter and the op-ed; and

(vi)

the June 9, 2021 letter from the Deputy Minister
of Conservation and Climate to Chief Spence and Dr. Halket in reply to the
April 8, 2021 letter.

[
8
]

The third order that TCN seeks would require production
from Manitoba of certain categories of records.  TCN says that these categories
of documents will show the extent to which Manitoba did not consult and failed
to accommodate with appropriate terms and conditions in the Final Licence.
Specifically, TCN seeks the production by Manitoba of the following categories
of documents:

(i)

the input received by the consultation team from
technical experts across government relating to concerns raised by TCN and
Manitoba’s responses and recommendations relating to those concerns and related
correspondence, as outlined on pages 40 – 41 of the Consultation Report;

(ii)

the input received from the Wildlife and
Fisheries Branch regarding a more ecologically relevant base flow for the
Churchill River at Missi Falls, as outlined on page 43 of the Consultation
Report; and

(iii)

the correspondence between Manitoba Conservation
and Climate (formerly Water Stewardship and Sustainable Development) and
Manitoba Hydro, in which the proposed Final Licence terms and conditions were
shared with Manitoba Hydro for its review and feedback, as stated on page 41
of the Consultation Report.

[
9
]

In arguing for this Court to dismiss TCN’s motion “in
its entirety”, Manitoba contends that with the three orders requested, TCN is
seeking to significantly expand the scope of the requisite Administrative
Record and Consultation Record on judicial review.  This expansion, says
Manitoba, would go far beyond what the common law in this province or elsewhere
in Canada has previously allowed.

II.

Issues

[
10
]

Given
the orders TCN seeks, the issues requiring this Court’s determinations can be
reduced to the following questions:

(i)

As it relates to Order #1, should this Court order Manitoba to
produce a copy of the Final Licence Record that is unredacted except where
necessary to protect solicitor-client privilege?

(ii)

As it relates to Order #2, should this Court order Manitoba to
include the six documents identified and described as being part of the
Consultation Record?

(iii)

As it relates to Order #3, should this Court order Manitoba to
produce the categories of documents identified and described by TCN?

[
11
]

After
a full consideration of all the evidence adduced on this motion, along with the
related submissions of the parties, I have determined that all of the above
three questions can be answered in the negative.  Accordingly and for the
reasons that follow, TCN’s motion for the three orders it seeks is dismissed.

III.

Background
and Context

[
12
]

In
its submissions, TCN makes certain assertions of fact without reference to the relevant
Record and to which, Manitoba states its disagreement.  In this connection, I
note that Manitoba maintains that it reserves the right to continue to disagree
with any factual assertions made by TCN on the merits component of this
application just as it reserves the right to challenge any extra-record
evidence TCN may later seek to adduce.

[
13
]

I
recognize that there is some dispute as to certain asserted facts that on the
merits hearing, will ultimately require resolution and determination.  Those
facts relate to the nature, breadth and scope of the consultation and
accommodation process.  Accordingly, nothing that I set out below by way of
background or context is meant to represent ultimate determinations or definitive
findings as it relates to the issues to be argued on the merits hearing.  That
said, for the purpose of considering this motion and facilitating its
disposition, what follows in the section below is what is nonetheless a
reasonable and objective contextualization of the CRD and AFP in respect of the
identified phases of what Manitoba says was its consultation process.  Despite
some of the anticipated disagreement as to certain facts that may have to be
addressed on the underlying merits application, the background that follows is
meant to assist in understanding the issues before the Court and the relief TCN
seeks on its present motion.

A.

The CRD and the Final Licence

(i)

The CRD

[
14
]

The
CRD was created to increase the water flow to large generating stations on

the lower Nelson River.  Most of the water flow of the
Churchill River is diverted at Southern Indian Lake into the Nelson River.

[
15
]

Construction
of the CRD began in 1973 and operations began in 1976.  The construction and
operation of the CRD was licensed pursuant to
The
Water Power Act

and the
Water Power Regulation
.

[
16
]

The

Water Power Act

has a three-stage licensing framework:

(a)

an "Interim Licence" to authorize development, construction,
and initial operation;

(b)

a "Final Licence" to provide for ongoing operation as built
and refined; and

(c)

a renewal process for the continued or proposed use of the water power,
waters, and land.

[
17
]

Pursuant
to section 43(1) of the
Water Power Regulation
, upon
completion of the initial development and upon fulfillment and compliance with
the terms and conditions of the interim licence, a licencee (such as Manitoba
Hydro) is "entitled" to receive a final licence.

[
18
]

Pursuant
to section 44 of the
Water Power Regulation
, the final
licence "shall embody the terms which were set out in the interim licence”
and such other terms and conditions as the Minister may impose.

[
19
]

Article
18 of Manitoba Hydro's Interim Licence states that upon due observance and
fulfilment of the Interim Licence conditions, the Minister "shall and will
issue in favour of the Licensee a Final Licence".

[
20
]

On
May 6, 2009, Manitoba Hydro requested the Minister grant a Final Licence
pursuant to the
Water Power Regulation
and terms of the Interim
Licence.

[
21
]

On May 12, 2021, following over ten years of consultation (described
below), the Minister granted Manitoba Hydro a Final Licence for the CRD.  The
Final Licence included new licensing conditions, as well as non-licensing
conditions that formed part of the Minister's covering letter to Manitoba
Hydro.

(ii)

The AFP

[
22
]

From 1986 to the granting of the Final Licence, the Minister, on an
annual basis, authorized Manitoba Hydro to deviate from the range of water
levels and flows stipulated in the Interim Licence.  That program is as earlier
noted, referred to as the "Augmented Flow Program" or
"AFP".  Each year throughout this period, Manitoba Hydro requested
the Minister's authorization of the AFP for the subsequent year.  The Minister invariably
granted that authorization.

[
23
]

In its application for the CRD Final Licence, Manitoba Hydro
requested that the terms of the AFP be incorporated, so that it would be
authorized for the term of the Final Licence to divert water from the Churchill
River on the same terms as the AFP.

[
24
]

The Minister granted this request in issuing the Final Licence.  The
Final Licence incorporates the same terms of the AFP that were granted by the
Minister annually under the Interim Licence.

(iii)

Environmental Impacts of the CRD and the AFP

[
25
]

The parties agree that the CRD has caused serious impacts to the
Churchill River and the Nelson River.

The parties do not agree on
the scope of those impacts or whether the AFP has caused any additional
impacts.

[
26
]

Manitoba Hydro (sometimes in conjunction with both the Government of
Canada and Manitoba) has entered into numerous agreements with affected
lndigenous communities and groups to address the adverse effects of the CRD and
the AFP.

[
27
]

TCN is a party to several such agreements concerning the CRD and AFP
(the "Agreements").  The Agreements provide: financial compensation;
mitigation and remediation measures regarding waters, lands, wildlife, and
fish; and cooperative natural resource management between TCN and Manitoba.

B.

Consultation for the Final Licence Application

[
28
]

Paragraphs 25 - 44 of TCN's brief provide a partial account of the
consultation process as it relates to the adequacy of Manitoba's consultation
with TCN.  Manitoba provides the following additional facts relevant to the
issues on TCN's motion.

(i)

Manitoba's Consultation Process

[
29
]

The CRD consultation process occurred with the guidance of a
steering committee with representatives from the Departments of Environment,
Climate and Parks ("ECP"), Indigenous Reconciliation and Northern
Relations ("IRNR"), and Justice and Finance (collectively the "Steering
Committee").

[
30
]

The Steering Committee identified Indigenous communities and groups
that may be adversely affected by the issuance of the CRD Final Licence and
established the level and scope of consultation with respect to each individual
community.

[
31
]

Manitoba ultimately consulted with 18 potentially affected
Indigenous communities and groups regarding Manitoba Hydro's Final Licence.  TCN
was one such community.

[
32
]

In accordance with Manitoba's standard practice, departmental staff
created and maintained a separate "Record of Consultation" for each
Indigenous community consulted, including TCN.  The Record of Consultation for
each Indigenous community

contains the following:

(a)      The
"Record of Communication", which logs all letters, faxes, meetings,
telephone calls, and emails that form part of the Crown-Indigenous consultation
process in relation to the Crown decision; and

(b)     the "Summary
of Concerns Table",

which lists the concerns that the individual
Indigenous community raised during the consultation process.

[
33
]

As affirmed by Ms Chelsea Silva, the Executive Director of the
Consultation and Reconciliation Branch within IRNR, Manitoba's view is that
disclosure of information that Indigenous communities provide to Manitoba in
confidence is harmful to the free and open discussions that must occur in
Crown-Indigenous consultation processes to advance reconciliation and
accommodate identified impacts.

(ii)

Consultation Capacity Funding

[
34
]

Manitoba offered consultation capacity funding for each community it
consulted as part of the Final Licence application.  All work plan and budget
offers made by Manitoba were made in compliance with the Consultation
Participation Fund Community Guide (June 2010) (the "Participation Fund
Guide").

[
35
]

Manitoba's objective in funding offers is to enable Indigenous
communities and groups to participate meaningfully in the consultation
processes.  The Participation Fund Guide provides for the funding of eligible activities,
including Community co-ordinator costs, honorariums, basic travel costs, hall
rentals, technical advisors, and other factors.

[
36
]

Pursuant to the Participation Fund Guide, when a provincial
department initiates a consultation process with a community, that department
will work with the community to develop a consultation plan (also known as a
work plan) and a draft budget that would outline anticipated community support
costs.

(iii)

Consultation with TCN

[
37
]

By the time the Minister issued the Final Licence, Manitoba says it
had engaged in over 10 years of consultation efforts with TCN.  Whatever
those efforts, Manitoba and TCN were unable to agree to a work plan and budget
throughout that period.

a)

Initial Consultation Process

[
38
]

ECP initiated the consultation process with TCN in June 2009.

[
39
]

In March 2011, ECP and TCN met for the first time. Manitoba had
previously attempted to contact TCN several times without success.

[
40
]

After the March 2011 meeting, ECP and TCN worked towards establishing
a work plan and budget.  TCN proposed a work plan and budget for $155,267 in
funding.  However, on November 23, 2011, TCN withdrew from the consultation
process after Manitoba made requests for further information regarding TCN's
proposed work plan and budget.

b)

2015 Re-Engagement

[
41
]

On four occasions between 2012 and 2015, ECP attempted to re-engage
TCN in the consultation process.  Finally, in February 2015, TCN agreed to
continue discussions about a work plan and budget.

[
42
]

On August 14, 2015, ECP sent TCN a proposed consultation work plan
and a budget for $48,922.90 in funding.  The work plan contemplated, amongst
other things,

three community meetings and the preparation of a
"Consultation Outcomes Report" by TCN with the assistance of a consultant.
TCN did not agree to the proposed budget and work plan.

[
43
]

Between February and June 2016, Manitoba and TCN met and
corresponded regarding developing a mutually agreeable work plan and budget,
but no budget came out of these engagements.

[
44
]

During this process, TCN tabled two work plans and budgets for
$149,445 and $149,866 in funding, respectively.  Significant portions of these
budgets were to cover professional fees.  The work plans contemplated seven
meetings and the preparation of an "Initial Assessment of Impacts
Report" and a "Summary Report".

[
45
]

On June 29, 2016, ECP wrote a letter to TCN stating, amongst other things,

that it was prepared to provide funding for the consultation
"components" it viewed as fair and reasonable at that stage of the
process.  Those components would have included:  an advisor to facilitate and
record discussion; two meetings; honoraria for Elders and Knowledge Holders; a
community coordinator; and an interpreter.  The letter attached a proposed work
plan and budget reflecting these components.  TCN did not accept this proposed
work plan and budget.

c)

2017-2020 Re-Engagement

[
46
]

In May 2019, the Minister met personally with TCN to discuss issues
relating to the CRD.  Following that meeting, TCN sent to Manitoba a new proposed
work plan for consultation on the Final Licence. TCN's proposed work plan did
not include a budget.

C.

O-Pipon-Na-Piwin Cree Nation ("OPCN")

[
47
]

In support of its motion, TCN relies on a redacted version of
Manitoba's Record of Communication with OPCN.  TCN received this document from
OPCN's counsel.

[
48
]

Most of OPCN's Record of Communication (as filed by TCN) has been
redacted except for those entries related to funding discussions.

[
49
]

TCN has not explained the purpose for those redactions or who
applied them.

[
50
]

OPCN's Record of Communication shows the following occurring in its
consultation process with Manitoba:

(a)

on January 11, 2017
OPCN tabled a budget of $358,669, which did not include certain "past
expenses";

(b)

on December 12, 2017,
Manitoba reviewed OPCN's previous work plans and budgets, and based on the
allowable timeline and eligible components, Manitoba proposed a work plan and
budget of $131,160;

(c)

on
May
16, 2018, OPCN proposed a budget of $255,236;

(d)

on July 18, 2018,
Manitoba sent an offer letter of a work plan and budget of $161,715.53, which
included $61,157 for certain past expenses.
Manitoba received no response to this proposed work
plan and budget.

[
51
]

TCN has not filed evidence of the underlying work plans and budgets
referred to in the Record of Communication, nor any other documents from the
consultation process

with OPCN.

D.

The Application Record

[
52
]

Following receipt of TCN's notice of application in this proceeding,
Manitoba prepared the two documents at issue in this motion:  (i) the Final
Licence Record; and (ii) the Pyles affidavit, attaching the Consultation Record.

(i)
The
Final Licence Record

[
53
]

The Final Licence Record represents the entire record of proceedings
put to the Minister in making her decision on whether to issue the Final
Licence pursuant to the
Water Power Regulation
,

subject to
certain redactions discussed below.

[
54
]

The Final Licence Record consists of a covering memo from the Deputy
Minister to the Minister and a Department of Conservation and Climate Advisory
Note (the "Advisory Note").  The Advisory Note attaches a
"Consultation Report" prepared to inform the Minister's licensing
decision.

[
55
]

The Advisory Note states that the Consultation Report "has been
prepared for the confidential consideration of the Minister and contains information
provided in confidence by communities."  Accordingly, in preparing the Administrative
Record, Manitoba made redactions to the Final Licence Record to withhold
irrelevant confidential information from Manitoba's
consultations with other Indigenous communities.

(ii)
The
Pyles Affidavit

[
56
]

The Pyles affidavit contains evidence responsive to TCN's allegation
that Manitoba inadequately consulted and accommodated it in respect of the
Final Licence.  Included as Exhibit D is a log of Manitoba's consultations
with TCN (defined as the "Consultation Log" but equivalent to the
Record of Communication defined above at paragraph 32) and available
records of those communications (defined as the "Consultation
Record").

[
57
]

Manitoba stipulates as part of its submission that the
"Consultation Record" attached to the Pyles affidavit is not found in
the Final Licence Record that was before the Minister in making her decision.

E.

TCN's Document Motion

[
58
]

Following the commencement of this proceeding, counsel agreed upon a
schedule for the filing of materials for the hearing of TCN's application,
including that:

(a)      Manitoba
serve the Administrative Record and an initial Consultation Record;

(b)     TCN send
to Manitoba any proposed supplements to the Consultation Record;

(c)      Manitoba
finalize the Consultation Record with any supplements that it agrees form part
of the Consultation Record;

(d)     TCN
serve and file all its supporting affidavits;

(e)      Manitoba
and Manitoba Hydro serve and file any responding affidavits; and

(f)      TCN
serve and file any reply affidavits.

[
59
]

Pursuant to this agreement, on July 27, 2022, Manitoba served the
parties with the redacted Final Licence Record and a draft of the Pyles affidavit,
including a draft of the Consultation Log and Consultation Records.

[
60
]

On September 22, 2022, TCN wrote to Manitoba to request:

(a)      that nine documents be added to the Consultation
Record; and

(b)     the table at pages 23 - 25 containing the
amounts offered to communities for capacity funding be unredacted;

(c)      production of "various documents that
informed Manitoba's decision making.”

[
61
]

Despite TCN’s assertions to the contrary (see paragraph 75 of
its brief), Manitoba maintains that it did agree to add certain documents to
the Consultation Record, but declined to add other documents that it did not view
as part of the consultation process with TCN relating to the CRD Final Licence.
Manitoba also declined to remove the requested redactions or to produce
documents that did not form part of the Administrative Record.  Manitoba
proceeded to finalize the Consultation Record by serving and filing the Pyles affidavit.

[
62
]

TCN's counsel then wrote to advise TCN would bring the present
motion because it needed to know "what is in the two records before we
finalize our affidavit evidence."

IV.

Positions
of the Parties

(i)

Position of TCN

[
63
]

TCN
contends that the three orders it seeks are justified in that they are relevant
to and/or required for the preparation of the judicial review merits hearing.

[
64
]

Respecting
Order #1, TCN argues that the redactions cannot be justified by Manitoba
as Manitoba cannot discharge its onus of establishing that the redactions are
clearly irrelevant and that the redactions are necessary to protect an
important interest or prevent significant harm.

[
65
]

Respecting
Order #2, TCN submits that Manitoba’s Consultation Record excludes
materials that were sent to Manitoba during the consultation process, which
materials expressed TCN’s concerns about the CRD and AFP.  TCN also submits
that the earlier identified matters (see para. 7) should be considered as part
of the Consultation Record.

[
66
]

Respecting
Order #3, TCN maintains that the documents that it seeks to have produced
are material and relevant to the question of whether Manitoba engaged in a
meaningful two-way dialogue with TCN regarding potential terms and conditions
of the Final Licence in order to accommodate TCN’s Treaty rights.  It is TCN’s
position that when Crown representatives formulate recommendations for the
decision maker, as a matter of procedural fairness, all parties must have an
opportunity to comment on them.

[
67
]

TCN
says that Manitoba did not adequately consult TCN on various matters, including
potential accommodations.  Production of the documents listed under Order #3
says TCN, would assist the Court in assessing the depth of Manitoba’s failure
respecting its consultation and accommodation, including on matters that TCN
suggests represent a gap in the procedural fairness afforded to TCN.

(ii)

Position of Manitoba

[
68
]

Manitoba’s
position on this motion is grounded in its basic assertion that TCN is seeking
to significantly expand the scope of the Administrative Record and Consultation
Record on judicial review, far beyond what the common law in Manitoba or
elsewhere in Canada has previously allowed.

[
69
]

As
it relates to Order #1, Manitoba contends that TCN seeks to expand the
relevant Record to selectively and inappropriately put before the Court parts
of Manitoba’s consultations with other Indigenous communities and groups that are
not parties to this proceeding.  Manitoba insists that consultations with other
Indigenous communities and groups are irrelevant to whether Manitoba satisfied
its duty to consult with TCN.

[
70
]

Respecting
Order #2, Manitoba resists TCN’s attempt to add documents unrelated to the
Final Licence decision and third-party communications (from religious
organizations to Manitoba) to the Consultation Record.  These documents are not
part of the Consultation Record in the Final Licence.

[
71
]

Respecting
Order #3, Manitoba once again resists TCN’s attempt to compel Manitoba to
produce internal government documents and communications that led to the
recommendations made to the Minister in the Final Licence Record.  Manitoba
argues that TCN is in effect, seeking documentary discovery of the deliberative
communications of public servants, notwithstanding the fact that those
communications were never before the Minister.

V.

Legal Framework

[
72
]

TCN
spends considerable time in its written submissions on this motion setting out what
it is correct to suggest is the well-established legal framework for the duty
to consult and accommodate.  In that connection, I do not intend in these
reasons to review or replicate TCN’s discussions of the governing law as set
out in paragraphs 76 – 96 of its written brief.  As it relates to this
legal framework, Manitoba states the obvious when it suggests that the legal
issues regarding the duty to consult and its discharge in this case are matters
to be decided at TCN’s application on its merits.  In agreeing with that basic
proposition advanced by Manitoba, I would add one additional nuance or
stipulation.  Insofar as some or any of the parts of the identified issues on
this motion need be decided on the basis of relevance and/or procedural
fairness relating to the obligations that flow from the duty to consult and
accommodate, it should be assumed that this Court is aware of and will remain
mindful of the governing law that will be applied at the merits hearing.  If for
the purposes of disposing of any of the issues on this motion, the specific
jurisprudence invoked by TCN requires particular consideration, those cases
will be identified and addressed in my analysis.

VI.

Analysis

i.

As it relates to Order #1, should this Court order Manitoba to
produce a copy of the Final Licence Record that is unredacted except where
necessary to protect solicitor-client privilege?

[
73
]

As
it relates to the first order that TCN seeks (Order #1), I have determined
that in the circumstances of this case, based upon the governing legal
principles and the evidence adduced, Manitoba has satisfied its onus of
establishing that it need not produce a copy of the Final Licence Record that
is unredacted.  More specifically, I have determined that Manitoba has
established that the redacted information is “clearly irrelevant” and that the
redactions are necessary to protect important interests and prevent harm.

[
74
]

All parties
agree that Manitoba has a common law duty to provide a record of proceedings on
a judicial review (see
Kalo v. Winnipeg (City of)
,
2019 MBCA 46
,
at paragraph
29
).  In the context of this underlying application, the
Final Licence Record is the record of proceedings.

[
75
]

It is accepted that this Court’s decision in
WSIB Investments
(Infrastructure) Pooled Fund Trust et al. v. Plenary Group (Canada) Ltd. et al.
,

2022 MBQB 145
, at paragraph
25
, establishes the applicable legal
principles for determining whether the redactions in question can be
justified.  See also
Duhamel v. Financial Institutions
Commission
,
2018 BCSC 601
, at paragraph
26
;
and
McGee v. London Life Insurance Company Limited
,
2010 ONSC
1408
, at paragraph
9
.

[
76
]

The applicable legal principles discussed in
the jurisprudence include the following:

(a)

relevant documents must be produced in their
entirety without redactions made unilaterally by the producing party;

(b)

redactions may be justified when the specified
portion is clearly irrelevant and the redactions are necessary to protect an
important interest or prevent significant harm; and

(c)

if a redaction is contested, the onus is on the
party requesting the redaction to establish, with evidence, that the redacted
information is clearly irrelevant and that there exists a sufficiently
important interest or potentially significant harm that will result from
disclosure.

[
77
]

To the extent that information about Manitoba’s consultation process
with other Indigenous communities and groups (and the funding Manitoba provided
in that regard) is found in the information contained in the redactions, such
information is irrelevant for the purposes of assessing the adequacy of
consultations with TCN.  Moreover, as was explained in Manitoba’s uncontested
affidavit evidence, disclosure of any such information could irreparably harm
Manitoba’s confidential consultation process with Indigenous community groups.
It should be noted as well that disclosure of such information would represent
a rather exceptional and significant expansion of the scope of the record on
judicial review of a statutory decision alleging inadequate consultation.

a)

Are the Identified Redactions Clearly
Irrelevant?

[
78
]

There are four categories of redacted information that TCN opposes.
In each of these categories of information, Manitoba contends that the
redactions are clearly irrelevant.  Those four categories relate to:
Table 2 – Budget Information; Table 1 ‑ Consultation
Table; Community Information; and AFP Information.

(1)

Table 2 – Budget Information

[
79
]

Respecting the Table 2 budget information — Table 2 contains information
for each consulted community concerning the date funding was approved, the
amount of funding approved and Manitoba’s comments on the approved funding.
Manitoba explains in its affidavit evidence that it has redacted the rows in
Table 2 concerning Indigenous communities that are not party to this
proceeding.

[
80
]

I accept Manitoba’s submission that although TCN argues that
Table 2 is relevant because it would show that Manitoba offered other
communities greater funding than TCN (which TCN argues would suggest that
Manitoba’s rejection of its proposed work plans and budgets was arbitrary), the
premise of TCN’s submission on this point is flawed.  The Record does not show,
nor does TCN allege that Manitoba rejected TCN’s proposed work plans and
budgets simply because the amount of funding TCN sought was too high or because
Manitoba was unable to fund the amount TCN sought.  Instead, it is apparent
that TCN withdrew its 2011 work plan and budget after Manitoba requested
further information.  It was also clear that Manitoba did not agree to TCN’s
2016 proposed work plan and budgets given what appeared to be duplication of
work and the number of consultant staff set out in the proposal.  What Manitoba
did do in response was to offer to fund “components” of consultation it viewed
as fair and reasonable.  Further, it would appear that TCN’s 2019 proposed work
plan did not include a budget or a proposed amount of funding.  As Manitoba’s
evidence suggests, part of the reason it did not agree to TCN’s 2019 proposed
work plan was because there was in fact no budget.

[
81
]

Manitoba is persuasive when it argues that the amounts of funding
offered to different communities based on different work plans and budgets and
agreed upon in different circumstances, is clearly irrelevant to the reasons
Manitoba and TCN did not agree to a work plan and budget.  The funding amounts
offered to Indigenous groups and communities is close to meaningless if
considered in isolation from the underlying work plans and budgets entered into
with those groups and communities.  Those work plans and budgets are not before
this Court.

[
82
]

In
Bigstone Cree Nation v. Nova Gas Transmission Ltd.
,

2018 FCA 89
, at paragraph
45
, the Federal Court of Appeal noted that the
Crown is under no obligation to provide consultation funding.  See also
Coldwater
First Nation v. Canada (Attorney General)
,
2019 FCA 292
(“
Coldwater”
).
The sufficiency of a consultation process will for the most part, be a factual
inquiry (see
Neskonlith Indian Band v. Salmon Arm (City)
,
2012
BCCA 379
, at paragraph
60
; and
Haida Nation v. British Columbia (Minister
of Forests)
,
2004 SCC 73
, at paragraph
62
.  That largely factual
inquiry will necessarily be specific to the Crown’s engagement with the
Indigenous group challenging the Crown decision.  It does not involve a
comparative exercise with other groups.

[
83
]

Manitoba is right to identify TCN’s erroneous reliance on Stratas
J.A.’s decision in
Coldwater
for the proposition that funding
amounts are relevant evidence.  In fact, Stratas J.A. held that where an
applicant alleges that the Crown failed to adequately consult, the Crown may
lead responsive evidence as to the capacity funding it offered as part of the
consultation process (see paragraph 17).  It is a rather stretched
interpretation of
Coldwater
to suggest that it stands for the
proposition that funding amounts offered to non-party Indigenous communities
are relevant as to whether the Crown should have offered more to the particular
Indigenous group seeking judicial review.

(2)

Table 1 – Consultation Table

[
84
]

A second category of information redaction that TCN wants disclosed
relates to Table 1 in the Consultation Table.  Table 1 summarizes
information relating to Indigenous community participation in the consultation
process, including when consultations were initiated and the dates of meetings
that were held.  In respect of this information, Manitoba has redacted those
rows that touch communities that are not party to this proceeding.

[
85
]

It is TCN’s position that the redacted information in Table 1
is relevant given that in conjunction with Table 2, it would likely show
the impact that the absence of a work plan and budget had on the consultation
process, including for example, the fact that there were no community sessions
held for TCN.

[
86
]

I again accept Manitoba’s submission that if Table 2 remains
redacted, for its part, Table 1 is also clearly irrelevant.  In the
present case, based on the evidence before the Court, Manitoba did in fact
offer TCN a work plan and budget that would have included funding for community
meetings.  It was TCN who chose not to engage in the consultation process on
the terms that Manitoba put forward.  Manitoba insists that had TCN chosen to
engage, there would have been funding for those community sessions.

[
87
]

In the end, I am persuaded by Manitoba’s submission that the
information in Table 1 would, at most, show that communities that agreed
to work plans and budgets with Manitoba went on to engage in the consultation
process.  TCN, which did not agree to a work plan, did not.

(3)

Community Information

[
88
]

The next category of redactions that TCN opposes are those which
contain information provided to Manitoba by Indigenous communities not party to
this case.  TCN’s submission is that production of this information ought to
occur “to the extent such information would shed light on the adequacy of
Manitoba’s consultation with TCN”.  As Manitoba has noted, this request by TCN is
not accompanied by any concrete justification as to why this information might
shed light on the adequacy of Manitoba’s consultation with TCN.

[
89
]

I am once again persuaded by Manitoba that the reason this
information has been redacted relates to its confidentiality and further, it is
clearly irrelevant to the adequacy of Manitoba’s consultation with TCN.  As I
noted earlier, consultation is not a comparative exercise and the adequacy of
Manitoba’s consultation with TCN should only be judged on the record of TCN’s
consultation process.  Even in cases where multiple Indigenous groups challenge
a particular decision, a court will assess the adequacy of consultation for
each group (see
Tsleil-Waututh Nation v. Canada
(Attorney General)
,
2018 FCA 153
(“
Tsleil-Waututh
”), at
paragraphs
575 – 597
).

(4)

AFP Information

[
90
]

The fourth and last category of redactions that TCN seeks to have
disclosed, relate to the redaction of the three bullet points at page 55
of the Final Licence Record concerning the financial impacts of not renewing
the AFP for one year.

[
91
]

This aspect of TCN’s argument can be disposed of quickly.  It would
seem that the financial impacts of not renewing the AFP was but one of several
reasons for incorporating the AFP as a term of the Final Licence.  Manitoba is
correct to argue that the specific monetary amounts at issue are irrelevant.

b)

Are the redactions necessary to protect
important interests and prevent harm?

[
92
]

I note that all of the redacted information to which TCN seeks
access consists of third party confidential information.  As Manitoba
underscores, other than two bullet points relating to Manitoba Hydro’s
information, most of the information consists of the confidential information
of other Indigenous communities not party to this judicial review.

[
93
]

As it relates to Manitoba Hydro’s confidential business information
that was provided to Manitoba in confidence, there can be no doubt that the
general commercial interest of preserving confidential information is indeed an
important interest to protect (see
Sierra Club of Canada v. Canada
(Minister of Finance)
,
2002 SCC 41
, at paragraph
55
; and
Sherman
Estate v. Donovan
,
2021 SCC 25
, at paragraph
41
).

[
94
]

As it relates to TCN’s request for the production of an
Administrative Record containing the confidential information of other
Indigenous communities, Manitoba calls this request “novel”.  Although TCN
appears to accept that it is Manitoba’s practice to treat the Record of
Consultation as confidential and that Indigenous communities ordinarily demand
confidentiality before participating in consultation, it (TCN) nonetheless
argues that the withheld information is not properly designated as confidential
given that much of its nature is “anodyne” and that its disclosure would
accordingly not cause harm to the concerned communities.

[
95
]

In making the arguments it does in respect of this aspect of the
test concerning the potential justification of redactions, TCN has not cited
any cases that would support the removal of such redactions relating to the
production of an Administrative Record containing the confidential information
of other Indigenous communities.  Indeed, their argument appears to ignore the
decision in
M
étis Nation of Alberta Association of Fort McMurray M
étis Local Council 1935 v. Alberta
,
2021 ABQB 282
, at paragraph
103
, in which the Alberta King’s
Bench rejected the applicant Indigenous community’s motion for unredacted
copies of documents that contained information submitted by other Indigenous
communities respecting a potential duty to consult that community.

[
96
]

TCN’s argument that the withheld information is not truly
confidential and that much of it is “anodyne” deemphasises the point about
which Manitoba urges this Court to appreciate:  that it (Manitoba) treats all
information received during the consultation process as confidential and that
appropriately, Manitoba leaves it to Indigenous communities to decide whether
disclosure of their information may cause harm.  In my view, Manitoba persuasively
contends that it is not for TCN to decide what information may be “anodyne” or
pose a serious risk of harm.  Further says Manitoba, it is not reasonable for
TCN to ask Manitoba “to make a unilateral, content based, subjective assessment
of information from and about Indigenous communities and groups not party to
the proceeding”.

[
97
]

In addition to the above submissions by Manitoba, which I accept, I
also note Manitoba’s supporting evidence that the disclosure of the redacted
information would in fact harm Manitoba’s relationship with Indigenous
communities who have come to expect that their information will remain
confidential.  What Manitoba realistically identifies as a harm flowing from
the connected reasonable expectation for confidentiality on the part of
Indigenous communities, provides a reference point for identifying what
Manitoba suggests could be threatened in terms of what need be the free, open
and reconciliatory discussions necessary for Crown‑Indigenous
consultations (see affidavit of Chelsea Silva, sworn February 21, 2023, at
paragraph 9).  Retaining the integrity, freedom and openness of these
reconciliatory discussions is appropriately noted by Manitoba as an important
public interest and it is the reason why Manitoba says its standard practice is
to refuse requests under the
Freedom of Information and Protection of
Privacy Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. F. 31, for confidential
Indigenous community information.

[
98
]

In a constructive suggestion for obtaining the information it seeks,
TCN has suggested as an alternative measure, that an unredacted version of the Final
Licence Record be filed in this Court under seal.  While I have examined the
suggestion with interest and an open mind, I remain persuaded by Manitoba’s
submissions that this alternative measure would not avoid the harm to the
identified public interest.  As Manitoba says, under this alternative,
confidential community information would still be disclosed to TCN (a third
party to those consultation processes) for a purpose other than the
group-specific consultation process in which the information was provided.  The
potential consequential harm would accordingly remain:  the undermining of
Manitoba’s relationship with the Indigenous communities with whom it seeks to
engage in reconciliation advancing Crown‑Indigenous consultations, which
require a requisite level of free and open communication.

[
99
]

Accordingly, for the foregoing reasons, as it relates to TCN’s
requested Order #1, this Court will not be ordering Manitoba to produce a
copy of the Final Licence Record that is unredacted.

ii.

As it relates to Order #2, should this Court order Manitoba to
include the six documents identified and described as being part of the
Consultation Record?

[
100
]

TCN’s requested relief seeks the inclusion of documents (identified
collectively by Manitoba as the “proposed records”) in the Consultation Record
that consists of:  i) letters between TCN and the Deputy Minister of
Conservation and Climate regarding the AFP; ii) TCN and OPCN’s open letter to
Manitoba Hydro customers and the op-ed in the
Winnipeg Free Press
; and iii)
correspondence from religious groups to the Minister.

[
101
]

The effect of the Order that TCN seeks, is to ask that a Crown’s
affiant swear a new affidavit attaching additional records that the Crown does
not consider part of the “Consultation Record”.  TCN cites no authority to
support the order it seeks and instead, invokes the Court’s inherent
jurisdiction to ensure the whole Administrative Record is brought before the
Court.  In arguing as it has, Manitoba is right to contend that TCN conflates
the Administrative Record and the Consultation Record.  In the Manitoban
context, the Administrative Record consists of all the material that was before
the original decision maker.  The corollary is that evidence that was not
before the initial decision maker is not generally admissible on judicial
review (see
Kalo
, at paragraphs
30 – 31
).  Although
providing no applicable jurisprudential authority for what it seeks in
Order #2, TCN at paragraphs 103 and 104 of its brief does rely on the
guidance of this Court and the Manitoba Court of Appeal in
Pimicikamak et
al. v. Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Manitoba et al
.,
2018 MBCA 49
;
and
Pimicikamak et al. v. Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Manitoba et
al
.,
2014 MBQB 143
, at paragraph
52
, respecting when extrinsic
evidence is admissible to supplement the Administrative Record on a judicial
review.  Despite TCN’s invocation of the above cases, Manitoba is again correct
in noting that TCN is conflating the Administrative Record and the Consultation
Record.

[
102
]

Insofar as the decisions in
Pimicikamak

have relevance to the present case, those decisions point to what Manitoba
characterizes as the appropriate and permissible route for TCN to have these
documents put before the Court.  That appropriate route is to lead its own
extra-record evidence by way of affidavits that establish the proper
evidentiary foundation for their admissibility.  See also
Manitoba Métis
Federation Inc. v. Brian Pallister et al.
,
2019 MBQB 118
, at
paragraph
67
.

[
103
]

I have determined that the requested Order #2 cannot be
justified and in any event, for the reasons advanced by Manitoba, the proposed
records or documents are not related to the Final Licence consultation process.

iii.

As it relates to Order #3, should this Court order Manitoba to
produce the categories of documents identified and described by TCN?

[
104
]

Through its requested Order #3, TCN seeks production of
documents that it acknowledges are not part of the Final Licence Record or the
Consultation Record.  TCN seeks to compel Manitoba to produce internal
government documents and communications that led to the recommendations made to
the Minister in the Final Licence Record.  Put simply, TCN is seeking
documentary discovery of the deliberative communications of public servants
despite the fact that those communications were never before the Minister.  In
making the request it has, TCN has provided no compelling reason for such an
exceptional order, which Manitoba accurately describes as having the potential
to turn the application into a hearing
de novo
based on the
deliberations and discussions of public servants, rather than the record of
materials before the Minister and record of consultations that occurred.

[
105
]

Discovery is generally not available in proceedings commenced by
notice of application (see
Jewish Community Campus of Winnipeg Inc. v.
Metaser et al.
,
2013 MBQB 303
, at paragraphs
5 – 7
).  While this
Court can order production of documents in an application as part of the Court’s
inherent jurisdiction to control and regulate its own procedure, absent any
right to documentary disclosure, the Court should only order a tribunal (whose
decision is under review) to produce documents that are actually admissible or
potentially admissible as extrinsic evidence (see
Jewish
Community Campus
, at paragraphs 6
and 21).  Given that it is well established that a judicial review is meant to
be a review of a decision and not a
de novo
hearing, on a judicial
review, any such extrinsic evidence may be introduced only in very limited
circumstances mindful of the established exceptions to
the general rule (see
Pimicikamak
(QB), at paragraph 52)
.

[
106
]

It is not clear how TCN can justify the documentary discovery it
seeks as admissible extrinsic evidence.  Given that the documents TCN seeks
were not before the Minister when she made her decision and given that they
were documents prepared internally for information purposes that were used to
consider the merits of various options, were these documents to be
characterized as admissible, the production and admission of them would
transform the application into a hearing
de novo
.

[
107
]

When I examine the nature of these documents and the jurisprudence
relied upon by TCN in their request for Order #3, I am not persuaded by TCN’s
position.

[
108
]

Manitoba is on solid ground when it contends that a decision maker’s
internal files do not form part of the Administrative Record provided they did
not otherwise form part of the proceedings (see D. Brown and J. Evans,
Judicial
Review of Administration Action in Canada
, §6:61 (Thomson Reuters Proview).  In
Waverley (Village) v. Nova
Scotia (Acting Minister of Municipal Affairs)
,
1993 CarswellNS 201,
[1993] N.S.J. No. 238 (CA), at paragraphs 18 – 20, and 23
, the Nova Scotia
Court of Appeal held that briefing notes not before the minister and documents
referred to but not provided to the minister are not part of the administrative
record.

[
109
]

In support of its position for Order #3, TCN relies upon
Tsleil-Waututh
;
Gitxaala Nation v. Canada
,

2016 FCA 187
; and
Manitoba Métis Federation Inc. v. The Government of
Manitoba et al.
,
2018 MBQB 131
(“
Manitoba Metis Federation Inc
.”).

[
110
]

TCN asserts that when Crown representatives
formulate recommendations for a decision maker, as a matter of “procedural
fairness” all affected parties must have an opportunity to comment on those
recommendations.  To the extent that TCN reproduced a quote from
Gitxaala
Nation
(but inadvertently referenced
Tsleil-Waututh
)
Manitoba argues that neither that case, nor any of the other jurisprudence
cited stands for or supports the proposition TCN asserts.

[
111
]

In its discussion of the jurisprudence,
Manitoba is right to clarify that in
Gitxaala Nation
, the Federal
Court of Appeal held that the parties to that proceeding would have an
opportunity to comment on a minister’s recommendation to the Governor in Council,
a statutory step that must be taken pursuant to the
National Energy Board
Act
, R.S.C., 1985, c. N-7.  Manitoba stresses that there is no
equivalent statutory process under
The
Water Power Act
.  In other
words, a minister exercising a statutory power to recommend the matter to the
Governor in Council is distinguishable from the internal deliberations of
ministerial staff (as part of a consultation process) that were never provided
to the Minister.  In addition, Manitoba distinguishes the Federal Court of
Appeal’s comments on the basis that they were limited to the party’s
participatory rights as part of the administrative process under the
National
Energy Board Act
.  In
Gitxaala Nation
, the court did not
address an applicant’s subsequent right to discovery in a judicial review
proceeding.  With these distinctions in mind, Manitoba submits and I agree,
that it does not support the relief TCN seeks.

[
112
]

In arguing that there exists a broad right to
discovery in a judicial review application, TCN relies on this Court’s decision
in
Manitoba Métis Federation Inc.
Despite TCN’s submissions, in
Manitoba
Métis Federation Inc.
, this Court cannot be seen to have established a
broad right of discovery in judicial review applications.  Such a reading of
that case would suggest a clear inconsistency with the many decisions that this
Court has rendered asserting and reasserting that judicial review applications
are not a hearing
de novo
even in cases assessing the adequacy of
consultation with Indigenous communities where admittedly, certain evidentiary
exceptions respecting extrinsic evidence may continue to evolve.

[
113
]

In rejecting TCN’s reliance upon
Manitoba
Métis Federation Inc.
as support for Order #3, Manitoba for its
part, points to that case as providing support for its position that the
internal documents to which TCN seeks production are irrelevant and should not
be produced.  In that decision, the applicant sought production of “advisory
notes and internal emails” prepared by Manitoba in preparation for an alleged
statutory decision.  This Court held that advisory notes and emails prepared internally
for information purposes were irrelevant to the issues on judicial review and
specifically, to whether the applicants were given sufficient opportunity to be
heard in advance of the decision (see
Manitoba Métis Federation Inc.
,
at paragraph 45).  In that case, this Court went on to note that the
nature of the documents were such that they are not normally subject to a right
of access.  Such are documents “touching upon governmental advice, analysis and
options which are normally used by government bodies to freely consider the
merits of various options” (at paragraph 45).

[
114
]

In the present case, the documents that TCN
requests are documents that were prepared internally for the purpose of
providing ministerial advice and are used by ECP to consider options before
preparing a recommendation to the Minister and any accompanying advisory materials
regarding the Final Licence Decision.  As such, I am of the view that they are
not relevant to the central issue of the adequacy of consultation.  Further, I
accept Manitoba’s submission that if disclosed, such disclosure would be
harmful to the free and open discussions necessary for public servants to
internally consider different options to accommodate Indigenous communities and
groups.

VII.

Conclusion

[
115
]

For the foregoing reasons, TCN’s
motion is dismissed.
